title: Let's Debate the AI Bans
author: Petrilli, Mike
summary: Mike Petrilli surveys the sudden wave of blanket K-12 AI bans in New York City and Los Angeles and uses them to stage a genuine debate rather than take a settled side. He presents the techno-optimist case (Michael Horn's warning that blanket bans punish parents actively choosing AI-forward schools, and Dacia Toll's Coursemojo as an example of AI built with instructional guardrails and teacher control) against a mounting body of evidence he finds hard to dismiss: a new Fordham/Impact Research survey in which 76 percent of students admit some illicit tech use and 26 percent admit using AI to cheat, and fresh PISA 2025 data showing OECD reading, math, and science scores at their lowest recorded levels, with heavy AI-using students scoring the equivalent of a year and a half behind non-users. Petrilli leans especially on an MIT-derived argument, relayed by Halina Bennet, that the entire purpose of K-12 schooling is to build students' capacity to read, think, and reason independently through 'productive struggle,' which is precisely the struggle unsupervised AI use removes — making New York's ban, in this framing, a defense of school's foundational purpose rather than mere technophobia. He closes by putting the burden of proof on ed-tech advocates to demonstrate AI tools that add real value without replacing student thinking, and by asking pointedly why other districts shouldn't follow New York and Los Angeles in pressing pause for at least a year.
points: New York City (grades K-8) and Los Angeles (K-12) have implemented blanket AI bans in schools, prompting a live debate Petrilli stages between techno-optimists and skeptics rather than resolves outright.

A new Fordham Institute survey (Impact Research/UpONE Insights) found 76 percent of students report illicit tech use at school and 26 percent admit using AI to cheat on tests or quizzes, often on school-issued devices.

Citing an MIT report relayed by Halina Bennet, Petrilli argues K-12 schooling's core purpose is building students' capacity for independent reasoning through 'productive struggle,' which unsupervised AI use directly short-circuits.

New PISA 2025 results show OECD reading, math, and science scores at their lowest recorded levels, with students who use AI very frequently for schoolwork scoring the equivalent of about a year and a half of education behind non-users, adjusted for socioeconomic status.

Dacia Toll's Coursemojo is offered as a counter-example of AI adoption done well: built with explicit instructional design, guardrails, and human teachers controlling what good instruction and questions look like.
quotes: We should be very wary about promoting blanket bans. Not only is it out of tune with the reality that some parents are intentionally opting for schools that leverage AI, but it will also limit the use in cases where ed tech makes sense in traditional schooling models.
76 percent of students report some sort of illicit tech use at school, often on school-provided Chromebooks or iPads. 26 percent of students report using AI to cheat on tests or quizzes.

Public K-12 systems are designed to produce in students the basic cognitive capacity to read, think, reason, and work through problems independently. That purpose is the exact thing that unsupervised A.I. use is best at overriding in a young person's development.
For a child, developing the ability to struggle productively is the entire point of school, making A.I., by M.I.T.'s estimate, a threat to the purpose.
Students who never use AI scored 509 on a science test, vs. 481 for students who use it very frequently-the equivalent of about a year and a half of education when adjusted for socioeconomic status

Show us the student-facing AI tools that you think can add real value to their learning without replacing thinking, and convince us that ordinary American schools can enforce the difference between the good and the bad
